Welcome to November’s edition We know that Shepley is an ancient settlement, described in the Domesday Book in 1086 as “waste” after the Harrying of the North in 1069/70. However, less than two hundred years later in 1217, Shepley seems to have recovered with the names of local landowners appearing in feudal records. Shepley then progressed through the Middle Ages with agriculture being the primary source of work and later the weaving of cloth and tailoring. In the Victorian era the village woke to the industrial revolution, with the railway arriving in 1850 and Shepley boomed. Featured in this issue: Church Services Info p6 & p7 FOSFS Christmas Fair p12 Woodley School p23 Bird & Wildlife Group p26 Cricket Club Awards p31 The Victorian and Edwardian periods were a time of great development in the village. Many of the fine stone houses and pubs that we see today were built at that time. There was some construction in the late sixties and early seventies but nothing particularly large scale until now when planning applications for new developments have soared, not just in Shepley but throughout our local region. We are now talking about several hundred proposed new properties throughout our area. Shepley and the other villages concerned will be changed forever with increased pressure on our roads and local services. New houses are needed, but is the destruction of ancient green land a positive or a negative thing? Please let us have your comments to our letters page. Our local pubs very much represent the earlier times with their sturdy stone construction and names depicting Shepley’s agricultural past and industry. What could be better in a village like ours than traditional pub names like The Farmers Boy, The Black Bull and even The Sovereign which represents the founding of Seth Senior’s famous village brewery. The one village pub which could do with a new name is The Cask and Spindle (previously The Railway Hotel). Although it’s been closed for seven years, the brewery has recently received planning consent for exterior lighting so a renaissance might be on the cards. Let’s hope a new village appropriate name goes with it. How about The Shepley Lion as the famed but mysterious beast was first reported to the police in a phone call from this pub where it had reportedly been seen in the car park, (could it have been a Jaguar) in 2011? Anyway, it kept the police busy for a few hours and train passengers were not allowed to leave the luxury of their carriages parked at the station where it had also been spotted (no it wasn’t a Leopard either). So, there’s a unique piece of Shepley history waiting to be immortalised. That elusive creature was reported the day after bonfire night in 2011, which brings us to our village’s favourite annual event at the cricket field on November the 5th as usual. Brian has been busy for weeks now building the giant structure and he and the whole cricket club team deserve our thanks for putting on this fantastic event every year. There is one important request here, please leave your car at home if you possibly can. If you walk to the event, you will have a far easier time and won’t have to worry about receiving a ticket from the police. On this night of all nights, it’s important that emergency service vehicles can safely navigate the road. There’s an article in this month’s issue from the cricket club with full information on this spectacular event. Shepley Women’s Institute Our clubs continue to keep busy At a recent members’ meeting we had a fascinating presentation by our very own ‘Man from Del Monte’, tea and coffee buyer Paul Jefferies, who taught us about processes to encourage sustainable tea and coffee farming and how Fair Trade organisations work to support young, female farmers across the globe. Our clubs have been busy as usual. The Strollers enjoyed a gentle, though slightly wet walk around the lanes at Farnley Tyas, finishing with what was intended to be a light lunch at The Golden Cock, though I have it on good authority that several portions of sticky toffee pudding were consumed! The Gardening Group cut back the hedging shrubs at the entrance to Shepley Health Centre to allow better visibility for drivers exiting the car park. They hope to return in spring to give the Cornus shrubs a good prune to encourage more red stems next autumn. Crafts and Crumbs members are busy working on a variety of personal projects, including embroidered pictures and cushions, knitted Christmas baubles and crochet throws, to name a few. It’s great that we have such a range of skills in this group as there is always someone on hand to help pick up dropped stitches, sort out tangled threads and occasionally unstick glued together fingers! Our next members’ meeting is scheduled for 2.00pm on Wednesday 18th November, when we hope to enjoy a practical Christmas crafts activity. However, we are unable to confirm at this point that the meeting will go ahead, as, at the time of writing, we do not have an incoming committee to take over following our AGM. As explained in the October article, most of us have already ‘served our time’ on the committee (some doing several stints over the years!) and many members have other commitments which prevent them from stepping up. As the timing of our AGM is after the 12th October deadline date for submission of this article, the result of the voting will not be published until December, but, whatever the outcome, we will keep you informed!

Shepley Naturalists’ Society The year turns WENTWORTH CASTLE STROLL For the last outing of the summer season, a group of eight tackled the grounds of Wentworth Castle, in sunny if slightly blustery weather. Considering recent rainfall, the ground was firm, but the lack of water in the admittedly small lake was significant. No ducks or geese for once. Deer were spotted lazing under trees, but all without antlers. Perhaps the males were away on a stag do somewhere. There was a good display of autumn crocus (colchicum cilicicum), while many trees were hanging on well beyond their normal lifespan. Lunch was taken in the formal garden, followed by a visit to Stainborough Castle at the top of the site. Four intrepid members took the stairs to the top of the tower and enjoyed the views of the surrounding countryside. The restored conservatory was next, followed by ice cream at the cafe, rounding off a pleasant ramble. Graham Bennett DALE DYKE RESERVOIR - the first of our monthly winter walks. On a lovely sunny day in early October, we drove over to Dale Dyke reservoir situated off the Strines Road. Our walk started down the zigzag path below the dam embankment, passing the information board reminding us that this was the dam that collapsed causing a disastrous flood in Sheffield. Today this area is heavily wooded, and the path around the side of the reservoir has lots of tree roots needing a bit of care to walk on it. A few birds were calling, mostly robins, while a scattering of mallards were on the low reservoir foraging on the mud banks. As it is the start of autumn various varieties of fungi were to be seen, fly agaric with its red top and a number of blushing wood mushrooms. After walking up to the head of the reservoir we stopped for a sandwich overlooking the higher Strines Reservoir next to the very isolated cottage there. In the last few years, the cottage has been refurbished and is now lived in. Our path then followed the upper track where we watched a couple of buzzards soaring overhead, passed another house and then continued beneath a large well-maintained manor house. A diversion of the track near a farm took us past inquisitive goats, back to the road and thence to the car. Shepley Methodist Church Is something missing? A recent survey found that 5% of young people aged 16-21 have no close friends, up from 1% in 2014. A news article says that phubbing, (short for snubbing people by focussing on your phone) is destroying relationships. You can see this in people glued to their phones and oblivious to the world around them. Today’s “me, me, me” culture, where we’re led to believe that life is all about what “I” want or need, doesn’t help either. People seem to be losing the confidence and ability to form relationships. It’s no wonder mental health problems are increasing. It’s also not surprising that there’s a revival in Christian faith growing in this country and around the world. You see it in celebrities and sports people publicly praising God and in growing numbers of church attenders in our towns and cities (it takes a while for new trends to make it into the more rural areas, like Shepley). People are finding friendships, feeling valued and a sense of belonging in meeting with other Christians. Learning to look outwards, to care for others, brings unexpected joy. If you’re wondering if there’s something that you’re missing in life, you’re welcome to pop into our Oasis cafe on Monday or Friday afternoons, 1:30-3:30. Feel free to bring along some knitting, craft or puzzles to share or just yourself. You’re always welcome to join our services on Sunday mornings from 10:45-11:45 or our monthly Bible studies on the last Sunday of the month from 9:30-10:30. If you think there’s something else we could offer our community, please let us know. Harvest at Shepley Methodist Church The congregation at this year's Harvest were challenged as to how they might use their (symbolic)12 baskets of crumbs, hearing those were left over after Jesus had miraculously made sure some 5,000 + people had enough to eat, despite only five loaves and two fish being offered. There were generous donations of tinned and packet food for the Methodist Welcome Centre, where the food was distributed to those in need. After the harvest service everyone was invited to stay for a delicious homemade soup lunch followed by a variety of homemade apple puddings using the apple from the orchard. Voluntary donations for lunch raised over £500 for the charity WaterAid. Contact: Rev Sue Pegg - 07931 832456

St Paul’s Church Remembering November is the season of remembering. I always feel blessed to have the gift of memory when so many other people have limited or no memories, caused by either trauma or illness. We are blessed to be able to recall memories that bring us joy. Remember the days when we used to play outside as children; when we rode on our bikes and built dens. Remember when we got a new job, moved into our own place, maybe got married and had children. Remember the 50’s, 60’s, 70,’s 80’s, 90’s? maybe longer or more recent; the friends you’ve made, the jobs you’ve had, the cars you’ve driven; everything and everybody you have loved. Armistice Day falls within the Church’s season of remembering, after the festivals of All Saints (1st November) and All Souls (2nd November), during which we remember those whom we love but see no longer. Maybe you wear a poppy on and around Armistice Day. This is a deeply personal and individual sentiment. About five years ago my daughter gifted me with a beautiful, hand-made poppy. The lady who made them, made an individual poppy for each of the British service personnel who lost their lives during the Afghan War. My poppy is number; 167 of 454. I wear my poppy to remember Private Robert McLaren of The Black Watch, 3rd Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Scotland (3 Scots), who died in Sangin Helmand Province aged 20years on 12th June 2009. Although I never met Robert McLaren, he plays a large part in my life; I am somehow connected to him through the poppy I wear. Maybe you visited our Heritage Weekend in September and read about some of the people of Shepley who lived, worked and died here. The people of Israel in the Bible were good at remembering. They told and retold stories of their ancestors who had played an important role in their history. Both you and I do the same thing. We tell and re-tell the stories of those who have gone before us as a way of remembering. During this season of remembering, before we jump ahead to Christmas, let’s bring to mind all those whom we love but see no longer. Hear from our Advertisers I'm Tricia and I moved to Huddersfield in the summer of 2015 with my partner. I'm a jobbing musician and I conducted Shepley Band for many years, until very recently. I'm currently branching out into other areas. Two years ago I was far too fat and unhealthy, so much so that my GP referred me to a lifestyle / diet coach. As part of the deal, I was allowed access to the local leisure centre in Huddersfield for a free “try before you buy” fitness month. There was so much variety and I attended many different types of class and activity, finding the dance fitness most appealing. Zumba, in particular, was especially invigorating and satisfying. I still maintain my KAL membership and attend as many classes as I'm able. The experience was an utter revelation. Gradually, class by class, dance by dance, I got more energetic, fitter and thinner. I've found a fresh energy to life and it's fantastic. I'm hoping to bring this, accompanied by some infectious music, to the good people of Shepley. What I've started in Shepley is a chance to share some feelgood dance vibes. I was a bit nervous in my first class but, week by week, I'm gradually feeling much more at home. The church hall next to St Paul's, is central and accessible, a wonderful ideal space for this kind of activity. Soon, if enough folk are interested, I'm going to introduce chair-based Zumba and perhaps Chi Chi Fit, a dance exercise class based on Broadway-style routines and memorable show tunes. Why not come and join me on Thursday morning and show us all your moves? As strenuous or relaxed as you prefer to make it - it's better when you're dancing :-)

Reflections on …….. My time as an Evacuee in Shepley (Part 1) I was born in Fulham in 1938. I had two older brothers, John aged 13 and Graham aged 10. We were living in Pimlico and my brothers were attending Battersea Grammar School. Soon after war broke out my father was sent on active service in Palestine and later transferred to the Indian Army. On the 1st of September 1939 the boys were evacuated, with their school, to Worthing in Sussex. They attended school on half days as they shared the buildings with Worthing High School for Boys. To be near the boys, mother moved down to Sussex with me, and this is where my sister was born. In the middle of 1940, due to the Battle of Britain, Battersea Grammar School was re- evacuated to Hertford and mother returned to Croydon where she could look after my grandmother and great aunt. She decided, for my safety, to arrange a private evacuation in the country. So it was, that in February 1942 I moved to Smithy Hill Shepley to live with Mr and Mrs Dransfield. Mr Dransfield had been deafened in World War One trenches and worked as a night foreman in the woollen mill at the bottom of Stretchgates opposite Far Bank, Shelley. Mrs Dransfield was the homemaker, a fantastic cook, superb needlewoman and extremely house proud. Mrs Dransfield made all my clothes from recycled material. There was only one room upstairs and I slept in a small bed in the corner. I was not allowed upstairs except to go to bed. Mr Dransfield slept during the day and as the cottage was so small I was sent out to play with the other children in the village. I came back for my dinner and then for my tea - two trips down the “flags” and two trips back! The path was spotless and had to remain so! I spent a great deal of time in the fields off Jos Lane, picking wildflowers and blackberries in the autumn. I went down Stone Wood Lane to the stream where I ‘fished’ for tiddlers. Harvest time was great. Mr Dransfield would put me out of the window at the back of the cottage, with a big stick. As the tractor went round the field cutting the corn the rats would come out. I would chase them with my stick. The Rec was a great place as it had a seesaw and swings and up the hill was the reservoir. When it was wet, I would go to the farm opposite Smithy Hill and play in their barn. There were steps up to a loft where there was a wooden 3-seater loo! I have fond memories of attending the local school. The central hall seemed enormous, it was where we had our dinner at big trestle tables. These were long, with possibly 12 children on each side, the teacher one end and an older pupil the other. A pile of plates was placed by the teacher. Dinner would arrive in big metal containers, served out and passed down the table. It was wartime so we were expected to eat everything. My favourite was rice pudding and if you had been good, you were given the container to scrape out. Wonderful! On my final day, before returning to London I scraped out the rice pudding container.

We used trays of sand in which to practise forming our letters and digits, much as whiteboards are used in schools today. Once mastered we progressed to paper and pencil. There was a big clock in the small hall, and I learnt to tell the time at a very early age. The teacher would send a child out to find out the time and if you returned with the correct answer, you were allowed home 5 minutes early. I remember loving to hear the teacher reading stories and she also read poetry to us. In April 1945 I learnt William Wordsworth’s poem ‘I wandered lonely as a cloud’. Mr and Mrs Dransfield didn't read to me, but when I returned to Croydon after the war my mother did and she loved poetry too so we would recite Wordsworth’s poem together. Each year Mrs Dransfield would have a professional photo of me taken to send to my mother. We entered the school by separate doors and our coats hung in rows along the wall. There were no toilets inside, they were in a brick outhouse in the playground. The urinals were open to the skies, surrounded by a brick wall whereas the girls were in a covered outhouse. Needless to say, you kept well away from the urinals. The school is up a steepish hill and there was a very big brick wall by the playground. If you looked over this to the field below you could watch the goats. There was a cottage on Lane Head Road, opposite Firth Street where a lady sold sweets from her front room and I remember buying liquorice sticks from her. On one occasion the cockerel she kept with her chickens attacked me, which made me very wary of chickens. Angela Sexton (nee Stiff) To be continued

Friends of Shepley First School (FOSFS) Christmas Fair, Friday 27th November Grab a brew and catch up on what FOSFS has been up to since my last update… First of all, I want to start this month's article with a HUGE thank you to everyone who supported our Summer Fair! Letter from our Member of Parliament Working on issues raised by residents October is an odd month. Summer is truly over, with the days shorter without the run-in to Christmas giving them purpose. I’ve been glad to see communities across our area still active with scarecrow festivals bringing people together. With political parties having their conferences across the country, I’ve been able to spend more time at home focussed on local issues. I recently had a great meeting with local micro-businesses at Yummy Yorkshire to discuss what they need from me and the Government to help them thrive and grow. We spoke about our crackdown on late payments, which are holding back so many businesses: a great conversation in such a fantastic setting. I couldn’t resist the cakes! In Shelley, I was delighted to confirm that the Penistone Road, at the bottom of Far Bank, will now be included in the council’s upcoming programme of repair works. This follows concerns from local residents raised with me at my recent coffee morning in the village hall. Highways have confirmed that the crossing is not operating correctly and the necessary works have been raised with their contractor. There isn’t a confirmed date just yet, but I’ll continue to chase for an update and make sure this progresses as quickly as possible. I have also been working with local residents, Northern Powergrid, and GTC, to address recent, frequent power cuts that have had an unacceptable impact on people. Throughout my conversations with both organisations, I have been clear that the current level of service is not good enough; people should be able to cook dinner and watch TV without worrying about services cutting out and alarms going off. Since my meeting with them, Northern Powergrid believe they have identified the main fault, and begun communicating directly to customers, including through in-person community events. I want to thank their engineers, who have been working tirelessly to get this fixed, and am continuing to push for effective compensation for customers. I know the problems haven’t gone away fully, so please keep reaching out to me so I know where Northern Powergrid needs to be delivering more. Since I became an MP, I’ve been able to really help hundreds of local people with issues ranging from passport delays and unfair fines, to getting the NHS care they deserve and their education. Helping people like this is one of the best parts of the job and also helps me launch wider campaigns to help our community. It was local people reaching out to me directly that gave me the full picture when getting answers from Northern Powergrid and when I bring up important policy issues in Parliament I always mention the stories of residents. Woodley School Encouraging the development of horticultural skills Giants visit Woodley! Earlier this month, Giant Vegetables from the Harrogate Autumn Flower Show visited Woodley School & College, a specialist school for pupils with autism in Huddersfield. Paula Haley from the Professional Gardener's Guild (PGG) dropped in with prize winners grown by David Barker (PGG Vice Chairman) and other exhibitors to show the students the giants people have grown. Paula said, "I had heard that Woodley wanted to develop their pupils' horticulture skills and thought what an amazing opportunity to show students what you can grow and to encourage excitement and enthusiasm. We need to do more to promote horticulture and this is a fabulous way to do it! It was enough excitement just to put them in my car and to bring them home!" Mr Adrian Sugden (Headteacher) was delighted to accept such a "big surprise!" The staff at the school were equally amazed as the vegetables, including carrots, beetroot, marrows, leeks, onions, and pumpkins were wheeled up the path. Two of the individual vegetables weighed over 25kg. The vegetables went on display for the day and were shown to all the school classes alongside examples from a local supermarket for comparison. Some of the children also had the opportunity to harvest the seeds from inside the vegetables. Shepley resident, Miss Claire Thompson (Assistant Headteacher at Woodley), who also organised the surprise said, "How fantastic that David and the other exhibitors from Harrogate Flower Show wanted to support our students. We are very grateful and always welcome ideas like this from our local communities. We plan to use the seeds from these giants to grow our own next year! Careers information and experiences run throughout our curriculum, and this gave us a wonderful opportunity to talk about farming, horticulture and greengrocery as possible future careers for our pupils. Being hands on with the vegetables, touching and smelling them supports our pupils to develop their knowledge and understanding of the world around them." If any local business would like to support Woodley School & College in enriching pupils' experiences with real-life work encounters or experiences, please do contact Claire at the school.

The Mast Integrated Neighbourhood Teams The Mast primary care network (PCN) comprises of five member GP surgeries Shepley, Kirkburton, Skelmanthorpe, Dearne Valley, Lepton and Kirkheaton. Together we serve over 35,000 registered patients. Integrated Neighbourhood Teams (INTs) are multidisciplinary, collaborative groups bringing together health, social care, and voluntary sector professionals to deliver seamless, proactive, personalised care to local communities. They are a major government and NHS England initiative, designed to transform community health and care. The INT acts as a single point of coordination to make sure patients with complex medical, social or rehabilitation needs can return home with the necessary care packages rather than staying unnecessarily in hospital or being discharged to a nursing home and reduces the likelihood of re-admission. Key benefits for the multidisciplinary team include a better understanding of what each team does, improved collaboration, better communication and reduced duplication of work. The MAST INT was chosen as the first accelerator site in Kirklees, focusing on improving patient support after hospital discharge. Weekly meetings bring together multidisciplinary professionals from general practice, hospital, community, social care, mental health, and rehabilitation services to ensure all aspects of care are addressed. A snapshot of Shepley’s history Lydgate Road Pronounced as ‘Lidgit’ and even spelled as Lydgett, this road did originally have a gate on it. At the top of the road where it meets Station Road there are now modern houses, but there used to be some open land and a shop (right hand image). This combined grocers, confectioners and corn merchants was run by Joshua Wood and later after Joshua’s death by his son Frank. Adjoining the shop were one or two cottages and Joshua also had his own bakehouse. In December 1879 there was a small fire in the shop. An overheating chimney flue set fire to nearby cloth goods. Joshua, together with Police Constable Ingham managed to get the burning goods outside and doused the flames with buckets of water, but £100 of stock was destroyed. Fortunately, the shop had insurance. Further down the road was Lydgate House, another laith house (that combined accommodation for both the family and their animals), although this property had weaver’s windows on its upper floors. This house was later occupied by Walter Wortley, a merchant tailor. Pinfold Cottage was so named because it was sited near the pinfold, a place where stray animals were penned up. The gate may well have been part of this structure. At 4 Lydgate until about the 1950s there was a greengrocer called George Henry Heeley who used to go round the village selling greengrocery with a pony and shandy (horse and cart). Dyke Bottom was also marked on maps although its name too has had numerous spellings over the years. Clare Francis With thanks to Norman Smith and David Billington’s team (who completed and shared much of this thorough research). Page 25 Answer elsewhere in the magazine

Shepley Bird and Wildlife Group A Love for the Wild & Our Duty to Protect it Our October talk was given by PC Caroline Newsome – Kirklees Wildlife, Rural and Heritage Crime Officer, Badger orkshire Studies GroupGroup. Caroline was accompanied by Crime Tactical Delivery two representatives of the badger groups in Huddersfield and various examples of wildlife of the area (taxidermied!). Caroline began the talk by giving us some details about her background in the police where she has been in a variety of roles, and in her passion for wildlife and nature. Currently she has pets, chickens, fosters hedgehogs for Shelley Hedgehog group, and keeps eight disabled hedgehogs safe in her garden. It was made clear how difficult it is to investigate wildlife crime – there are rarely witnesses or CCTV evidence etc and of course the animals and birds cannot tell us their stories. We were given a list of the sorts of crimes and incidents that are investigated – and each one led on to a story about an example of these crimes. Some were very distressing to hear, but Caroline’s passion for her job and her stories of other kinds of incidents gave us relief from the difficulty of witnessing the cruelty that some people show. One of the most endearing incidents was of a badger – stuck on a roof! The house involved was on a steep hill, where the garden above was on a level with the roof concerned. The badger had clearly wandered off, fallen down a level onto the roof and was unable to get back up. Caroline and colleagues Sue, Rob and Fletch made a two-pronged rescue attempt – Caroline herself on a ladder at the front of the house trying to attract the badger’s attention with Sue holding her steady and Fletch and Rob up on the roof attempting and ultimately succeeding to get the very alarmed badger into a cage. Fortunately, the animal was rescued and released but unfortunately, the rest of that day was spent with one rescuer receiving treatment at A & E for a severe badger bite to the hand! There are a number of local organisations – like Shelley Hedgehogs and the Badger groups – that help out with the work that Caroline does and she acknowledged that she would find it extremely difficult to do her work without them. As always, the talk was greeted with a round of applause – with an extra appreciation for the difficulty of Caroline’s work, and how glad we are that she is there to do it! Cliffe House A celebration of creativity and community Dear Community, We are always really excited as Art at the House approaches and this year it took place at Cliffe House on Saturday 19th and Sunday 20th September. This time the feeling was a little different. With an expanded committee of five volunteers and with support from the outstanding Cliffe House staff we had much more to look forward to. With generous funding from Kirklees Seasons of Culture and Kirkburton Parish Council, along with sponsorship from several local businesses, we were able to expand onto the front lawn at Cliffe House and grow the woodland market into something really special. A stone monolith sculpture was permanently put in place by sculptor Ryan James and will be finished with your help over the next couple of years at the event. We finally managed to get a real piano into the woods which sounded magical! We introduced some new dimensions to the event but essentially, this was a celebration of creativity and community engagement. The feedback we have had from stall holders and the public has been overwhelmingly positive though we have learned some lessons which will help us to improve our planning for next year. Aside from a bit of rain on the Saturday morning the weather was kind and for the most part the sun came out and brought great vibes with it. We counted well over 2000 people at the gates over the weekend who came and took part in lots of workshops, listened to live music and bought quality art and crafts. Art At The House is a not-for-profit Community Interest Company and this year for the first time we asked for your donations to help us grow the event and you did not disappoint, thank you! As for this year’s event we would like to say a huge THANK YOU to you the Shepley community for supporting the event through thick and thin. We live in a very special village. https://artatthehouse.co.uk/ Follow us @artatthehouse Nigel Hoyle and the ArtattheHouse Team

Shepley Cricket Club Bringing the season to a close Our Senior Presentation Night brought the curtain down on another season at Shepley Cricket Club and gave us the opportunity to celebrate the achievements, commitment and community spirit that make our club so special. It is always one of my favourite evenings of the year. Whilst many of the trophies recognise performances on the field, it is also a chance to thank the many people whose contribution often goes unseen. Whether you've spent your summer playing, scoring, coaching, fundraising, preparing teas, serving behind the bar, maintaining the ground, or simply cheering the teams on from the boundary, you've helped make 2026 another memorable year for the club. (left) James Tate, 2nd XI Players’ Player of the Year; (centre) Connor Dale, 1st XI Players’ Player of the Year & Captain’s Player of the Year; (right) Teddy Hartley, 2nd XI Captain’s Player of the Year. It was particularly pleasing to see individual contributions recognised through awards such as the Trevor Curtis Trophy (Alison Rose) and Junior Clubman of the Year (Kitty Dawson), alongside the achievements of our senior and junior teams. It was also wonderful to celebrate our Huddersfield League-winning Under9s alongside the senior players. Seeing our youngest cricketers sharing the stage with our senior teams was a timely reminder that the future of the club is in good hands. Renovation work on the square is underway, with essential repairs and maintenance taking place to ensure it is in the best possible condition for the 2027 season. Also, anyone who has walked past the club recently will have noticed work beginning on our Nursery Ground, a project that has been the focus of so much fundraising and planning throughout 2026. Seeing diggers on site makes all those sleepless nights, fundraising events and grant applications feel worthwhile, although there is still plenty of work ahead before the project is complete. Whilst the club is seldom used during winter, this perhaps makes it even more important that we are keeping an eye on the little things. Keeping the building up to temperature, watching out for those little bits of damp that can, over a short period of time, turn a small issue into a big problem, and generally making sure everything is ready for when cricket returns next spring. Before we know it, thoughts will turn to winter nets and another cricket season. Until then, winter well, and we look forward to welcoming everyone back to Shepley Cricket Club in 2027. Matthew Hartley Chairman, Shepley Cricket Club
